files.source: Pinned TEST INPUT, not an oracle: the SAME INSDC record AF071878.1 as served by ENA in EMBL flat-file format, fetched once from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/api/embl/AF071878?lineLimit=0 and saved byte-for-byte. files.source: CRISPOR, tag v3.1, fetched once from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/maximilianh/crisporWebsite/v3.1/crisporEffScores.py and saved byte-for-byte. THE pinned definition of the on-target score this app names: `doenchParams` (the 70 singleton + dinucleotide weights of Doench et al. 2014 Nat Biotechnol Rule Set 1, PMID 25184501) and `calcDoenchScores`, which states the model's input contract in one line -- "Input is a 30mer: 4bp 5', 20bp guide, 3bp PAM, 3bp 5'" -- then applies intercept 0.59763615, the GC term (gcLow -0.2026259 / gcHigh -0.1665878, times abs(10-gcCount)) and the logistic 1/(1+exp(-score)). Verified identical to the same tables at the repository's master tip (both `doenchParams` and `hitScoreM` compare equal byte-for-byte), so the pinned v3.1 copy is not a stale variant.
files.license: Disputed by the upstream author's own two licence files, so BOTH are pinned alongside it and neither is paraphrased here. The LICENSE.txt at the v3.1 tag (crispr/CRISPOR-v3.1-LICENSE.txt) is Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 3.0 Unported. The LICENSE.txt at master (crispr/CRISPOR-master-LICENSE.txt) states retroactively: "Up to and including version 3.1, the source code files crisporEffScores.py and crispor.py were licensed under GPLv3." v3.1 was pinned rather than master precisely because master's own terms restrict later versions to academic use. Both files are reference authority under gx/corpus/ only -- nothing in backend/ or gui/ imports them, and no gx test imports them as Python either: the numeric tables are re-typed into gx/crispr/crispr_oracle.py, which asserts each one against these pinned bytes at import time. A reviewer who objects to CC-BY-NC sitting in an MIT repository can delete both .py files; the oracle keeps working and only the byte-level pin is lost.

files.source: CRISPOR, tag v3.1, fetched once from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/maximilianh/crisporWebsite/v3.1/crispor.py and saved byte-for-byte. Pinned definition of the off-target score this app names: `hitScoreM` (the 20 position-specific mismatch weights of Hsu et al. 2013 Nat Biotechnol, PMID 23873081 -- index 0 is protospacer position 1 at the PAM-distal 5' end, index 19 is position 20 in the PAM-proximal seed, weight 0.583), `calcHitScore` ("see 'Scores of single hits' on http://crispr.mit.edu/about", the three-term product score1*score2*score3*100 taken over the ACTUAL positions at which guide and candidate differ) and `calcMitGuideScore` ("Sguide defined on http://crispr.mit.edu/about", 100/(100+hitSum)). Also the pinned SpCas9 PAM convention: `pamDesc` line 91, ('NGG','NGG - Streptococcus Pyogenes'), and `DEFAULTPAM = 'NGG'`.

files.source: THE authority for this round: NCBI's genetic-code tables, fetched once from https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/misc/data/gc.prt and saved byte-for-byte. The ASN.1 text behind https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Taxonomy/Utils/wprintgc.cgi. Each table gives `ncbieaa` (the amino acid of all 64 codons) and `sncbieaa` (`M` at every codon that table calls a START, `*` at every stop), in the codon order the three `-- Base1/2/3` comment lines spell out: TCAG x TCAG x TCAG. Table 1 Standard starts are TTG, CTG, ATG; table 2 Vertebrate Mitochondrial reads TGA as W, ATA as M and AGA/AGG as stops; table 11 Bacterial adds GTG/ATT/ATC/ATA to the start set. gx/orf/orf_oracle.py reads the strings out of this file rather than trusting any Python copy of them, and cross-checks Biopython's tables 1/2/11 against it.
files.license: NCBI-produced data: a work of the U.S. Government, placed in the public domain -- https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/home/about/policies/ ("information that is created ... by NCBI ... is in the public domain"). Freely redistributable in this MIT repository.

files.source: Biopython 1.85, installed at /usr/local/lib/python3.11/dist-packages/Bio/Data/CodonTable.py. The machine-readable form of gc.prt: `register_ncbi_table` calls carrying each table's `names`, `id`, forward table, `stop_codons` and `start_codons`, exposed as `unambiguous_dna_by_id[n]` / `ambiguous_dna_by_id[n]`. Pinned as a second, independent rendering of the same authority -- gx/orf/orf_oracle.biopython_matches_gc_prt re-renders tables 1, 2 and 11 from here back into gc.prt's ncbieaa/sncbieaa strings and requires an exact match, so neither copy is trusted alone.

files.source: Pinned TEST INPUT and recorded-literal oracle: RefSeq NC_012920.1, the Homo sapiens mitochondrion revised Cambridge Reference Sequence (rCRS), 16,569 bp, circular, fetched once from NCBI E-utilities efetch (db=nuccore, rettype=gbwithparts, retmode=text) and saved byte-for-byte. Added for this round because it is the only real record that carries every hard case of the capability at once: 13 CDS features all declaring /transl_table=2 (vertebrate mitochondrial, where TGA is W and AGA/AGG are stops), six of them (ND1, ND2, COX3, ND3, ND4, CYTB) whose spans are NOT a multiple of three because the stop codon is completed post-transcriptionally -- real partial trailing codons, each declared with /transl_except=(pos:...,aa:TERM) -- and one N at 0-based 3106, the rCRS placeholder. Every CDS also carries a /translation qualifier, which is NCBI's own protein and therefore a recorded literal nothing in this repo produced: the gx tests compare against those 13 strings.
